Study

Exam nerves

Some nerves help you perform. When they block you, two simple techniques have shown an effect: reframing them and writing about them.

A racing heart, sweaty hands, an upset stomach and the feeling you have forgotten everything. Exam nerves are very common, and in some people they can block performance.

Why anxiety gets in the way

Worry uses up part of working memory, the mental space we use to reason and recall in the moment. If part of it is busy thinking "I'm going to fail", there is less left for the exam. But a moderate level of arousal can be useful: it helps us stay alert and focused.

Two techniques with support

In 2010, Jeremy Jamieson and colleagues told students preparing for an admissions exam that physical arousal does not hurt but can improve performance. Those who received this message scored better in maths than the control group, including on the real exam. This is arousal reappraisal: the idea is not to calm down, but to read the nerves as energy.

In 2011, Gerardo Ramírez and Sian Beilock asked students to write for ten minutes about their worries just before an exam. Their results improved, especially among the most anxious. Writing seems to free up mental space.

What usually helps

  • Study in advance and practise with mock exams: that is what reduces anxiety most.
  • Sleep well the night before, rather than studying late.
  • Breathe slowly for a few minutes before you start.
  • Begin with the questions you know to build confidence.
If anxiety is so intense that it stops you sitting exams or always blocks you, a psychologist can help.

References

  1. Jamieson, J. P. et al. (2010). Turning the knots in your stomach into bows: reappraising arousal improves performance on the GRE. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 46(1), 208–212.
  2. Ramirez, G. y Beilock, S. L. (2011). Writing about testing worries boosts exam performance in the classroom. Science, 331(6014), 211–213.
